directAnswer: Pope John IX was a Benedictine monk from Tivoli who reigned from 898 to 900. Through synods at Rome and Ravenna he formally annulled the Cadaver Synod, rehabilitated Formosus, banned trials of the dead, and required that papal consecrations take place in the presence of imperial envoys.

paras: John, the son of Rampoald, had been a monk of the Order of St. Benedict and was ordained priest by Formosus. After Theodore II's death, a faction hostile to Formosus put forward Sergius, later Pope Sergius III, but John's supporters prevailed, and he soon worked closely with Emperor Lambert. Sergius and his allies were excommunicated and driven from Rome.

Early in 898 John held a synod in Rome that confirmed Theodore II's decisions. It declared the acts of the Cadaver Synod void, ordered its records burned, restored the clergy ordained by Formosus, and prohibited the trial of anyone after death. It also condemned the irregular election of Boniface VI.

To prevent the violence that had marred recent elections, the synod decreed that a new pope should be consecrated only in the presence of imperial representatives. A second synod at Ravenna, held with Emperor Lambert, confirmed these measures and the rights of the Roman Church. Lambert's death later that year deprived John of a protector, and he also had to reckon with Hungarian raids in northern Italy. John died in January 900.

keyFacts: Born at Tivoli; a Benedictine monk ordained by Formosus
Elected over the rival candidate Sergius (later Sergius III)
Held synods at Rome and Ravenna in 898
Annulled the Cadaver Synod and forbade trials of the dead
Required imperial envoys at papal consecrations

faqs.question: How did John IX respond to the Cadaver Synod?
faqs.answer: His Roman synod of 898 declared it void, ordered its records destroyed, restored Formosus's clergy, and banned any future trial of a dead person.

faqs.question: Who was John IX's rival for the papacy?
faqs.answer: Sergius, an opponent of Formosus, was proposed by a rival faction in 898. He was excommunicated and exiled, but later became pope as Sergius III.
